label: Working With Diagrams
notes: This chapter turns tensor diagrams from a notation into a working calculus. We treat a diagram as a proof state: nodes carry coordinate data, wires carry contractions, and a rewrite is trusted only when an invariant survives it. The payoff is mechanical proofs of incidence theorems like Pappos and Desargues.

label: Diagrams as Proof States
notes: Remind students that epsilon nodes are three-legged determinant brackets and delta wires are plain index identifications. A closed diagram, with no free legs, evaluates to a projective scalar invariant. The whole game is rewriting the picture while keeping that scalar fixed, so vanishing is preserved.

label: The Epsilon-Delta Identity
notes: This is the engine of the chapter. A product of two epsilon tensors equals a signed sum of delta contractions, the determinant of a Kronecker matrix. Stress the alternating sign pattern: it is the antisymmetrizer made explicit. Every later reduction is repeated application of this one rule.

label: Reading the Identity as a Picture
notes: Walk through the diagram form slowly. Two three-legged nodes joined on one wire resolve into a difference of two parallel-pairing diagrams. Point at each pairing on the SVG. The sign comes from whether the pairing is order-preserving or swapped, which is the source of all the bookkeeping.

label: Brackets and Antisymmetry
notes: Connect the epsilon tensor to the bracket determinant students already know. Antisymmetry means swapping two legs flips the sign, and a repeated leg kills the bracket. These two facts, plus multilinearity, are everything needed to collapse a complicated diagram into a monomial in brackets.

label: Reducing to Bracket Monomials
notes: Describe the reduction loop: locate an epsilon-epsilon pair sharing a wire, apply the identity, expand into delta terms, and contract delta wires until only closed brackets remain. The endpoint is a signed sum of bracket products, a bracket polynomial, which is the canonical invariant form.

label: Trace-Zero as an Incidence Machine
notes: This is the notebook's first worked diagram. A trace-zero projective map sends the cross-meet of join(a,b') and join(a',b) back onto the original line join(a,b). The trace condition is the diagrammatic hypothesis; the incidence residual, numerically zero, certifies the rewrite was valid.

label: Pappos by Diagram Transformation
notes: Pappos is the showcase. Its collinearity claim becomes a closed diagram whose bracket expansion, after epsilon-delta moves, collapses to identically zero. Emphasize that no coordinates are chosen; the cancellation is structural. The same template, with a conic instead of two lines, gives Pascal.

label: Pascal as Join-Meet Program
notes: Show how six conic points and three opposite-side intersections reduce to one bracket condition. In the notebook the collinearity residual is near machine zero across a whole family of conic parameters. That stability is the visual signature that the diagram, not one lucky drawing, is carrying the theorem.

label: Conics, Tangents, and the Adjoint
notes: A symmetric matrix is the conic; its adjoint is the dual conic. A point on the conic has tangent line A p, and tangent lines satisfy the adjoint equation. Explain that this is exactly the diagram with two epsilon tensors and copies of the quadratic form, contracted down.

label: Rank-4 Diagrams and Plucker
notes: Move to RP3. A line carries six Plucker coordinates packed into an antisymmetric matrix, the covariant line tensor; the epsilon-dual gives the contravariant one. The Grassmann-Plucker relation is the antisymmetry-plus-epsilon statement whose zero residual certifies the six numbers are a genuine line.

label: Synthesis and Habits
notes: Close with the working discipline: every diagram rewrite is paired with a residual, trace, incidence, collinearity, tangency, antisymmetry, or Grassmann-Plucker. Two invariant expressions are equal exactly when their diagrams reduce to the same bracket monomial. That equality, made mechanical, is the chapter's deliverable.
